text: By now a real engagement has piled up a WHOIS record, subdomains from crt.sh, a theHarvester export, a Shodan result set, Nmap scans, and a handful of banner grabs. That's a lot of intelligence and almost no structure. This lesson closes Chapter 2 by turning all of it into one artifact: the attack surface map, the thing that actually tells you what your attack surface is.

Every row in a real map carries the same consistent fields: what the asset is, which source found it, what ports or services are actually open, and a note for anything that needs follow-up. That source field matters more than it looks — it's what lets you trace any finding back to exactly how it was discovered, which a professional report has to show for every claim it makes.

A simplified row might read: vpn.target.com, found via crt.sh, status confirmed. 10.20.30.15 port 22, found via nmap S S dash p dash, status confirmed, OpenSSH 8.9 banner-checked. A public S3 bucket, found via a Google dork, status unconfirmed until someone verifies what it actually contains. Three very different assets, discovered by three completely different techniques, sitting in one consistent structure that anyone on the team can read at a glance.

Not every finding deserves equal weight, so tag by confidence: confirmed means two or more independent sources agree, probable means one source and plausible but unverified, unconfirmed means a single weak signal that needs follow-up before anyone acts on it. And if an asset shows up that was never named in the signed Rules of Engagement, that's a stop-and-ask-the-client moment, not a line item to quietly fold in.

That map is the handoff into everything Chapter 3 covers. Every host and port it already lists becomes the input for deeper service and version enumeration — nobody re-discovers the same hosts from scratch. Reconnaissance and OSINT are done; next chapter, Nmap gets a proper deep dive, starting from exactly the map you just learned to build.
